commenti.body: 100% agree. film had about 5 opportunities to just finish and be a pretty good social commentary, but doubled down on its stupid twists so many times that eventually the whole experience feels like a really well shot waste of time.

I think a lot of the hate for this movie hinges on “I heard it was supposed to be….” which completely alters the experience of pretty much any film. I saw this film with absolutely no context for it whatsoever and it was a fabulous experience. Hot, weird, fun and engrossing. A lot like classic gothic romance IMO. But instead, people want it to be this brilliant philosophical masterpiece that pulls off some deep societal commentary. That’s not what this movie is trying to be. I don’t know, the reaction to the reaction of this film has really been something.

Potentially part of the reason it isn’t impactful is because it doesn’t have much to say, and what it does say at all is kind of backwards and misguided.

Emerald Fennell, the director and writer of Saltburn, comes from an insanely wealthy family, and basically grew up in the world of Saltburn (minus the psychopath).  So what we have is a story that appears to be about class, written by a person who was born into the highest possible class.  And she writes it from that perspective.  Yes, the rich family is comedically dumb and quirky, but compared to Oliver, they’re all relatively decent people, or at least normal people.  And for three fourths of the movie, Oliver is shown to be from the lower class.  And the movie makes a point of showing what a pathetic, greedy little freak the little lower class guy is.  But than there’s a curveball.  He’s actually from the upper middle class!  And now the movie becomes a “beware of social climbers” story, where the middle class is just jealous of the rich people, and will grovel and scheme just to get a taste.  For a film that seems to make a point of being about class, it has all the wrong things to say.

Now for me, I think that thematically, the movie works better as a tale of obsession and the dark nature of love.  But even than, it really doesn’t have much to say besides “if you love someone, you might do some crazy stuff”.  It’s thematically weak on all fronts, while trying to have a lot of complex themes.

I’ve seen Saltburn compared to Parasite, and I think that comparison is absurd.  They are monumentally different films, with parasite being leagues ahead of Saltburn.  I’ve been told that Bong Joon Ho came from a rather well-off family by Korean standards, but the difference between his film and Fennell’s movie is that he treats both classes with empathy and makes a point to show that every one of them is human.  No one is ultimately “better” than the other, and they all have issues, biases, and desires.  Yes, it’s a take down of the absurdity of the upper class lifestyle and it’s indifference towards the lower classes, but it still treats its “villains” as people, and that makes a world of difference.  Parasite is filled with empathy and a conscious desire to make a difference, while Saltburn runs off of condescension and preference towards shock over heart.  It wants you to remember it for its edgy/shocking scenes, not it’s substance.  And that’s fine, but Fennell should have made that clear from the get go rather than cramming her film with half baked themes and backwards commentary.

That being said, I enjoyed Saltburn from an entertainment perspective.  I thought it looked amazing, and the sound and editing were very good as well.  I enjoyed all the montages for what they were: fun, energetic montages.  And I thought it was fun watch overall.  But I absolutely think it is a shallow film that tries to hard to be shocking for the sake of being shocking.

It's a ridiculously shallow film, the sort of BS the pretentious students in the film themselves would think was deep.

It is well shot and acted, but the writing just has so little going for it. There isn't a single character of any actual interest, every one of them is a cliche that's been better done elsewhere.

It riffs off Ripley, Brideshead and Alan Hollinghurst's great novel The Line of Beauty. All of them are basically about social outsiders dazzled, then more or less rejected, by rich, beautiful people. Ripley is the closest in that he turns murderous and sociopathic.

The difference is, all of those were created by interesting people with interesting life stories who actually had something original to say, so all of them are masterpieces in their own way. They do vastly more with the premise than the shallow nonsense on display here, which just aims to shock for the sake of it.

If I might speculate, I'd suggest that the creators of all of those were themselves at one time or another in the position of the outsider themselves, very much unlike Fennell who instead is condescending to position Oliver as her protagonist, even though she only really knows a world like Felix. Which is as insulting as it is (predictably) a failure artistically.

It's fine to riff off a minor sub-genre, but for gods sake add something to it. Do something new or interesting that isn't just showy bullshit. Every one of Waugh's characters in Brideshead is a fully realised, profoundly tragic figure in their own right. By contrast, Fennell produces tedious, shallow bores with no inner life at all. The rich folks aren't remotely interesting here, and serve as mere ciphers. And don't get me started on the horrendous miscasting (Grant and Shearsmith are both completely bizarre choices that don't work at all, yes the latter is brief but it's a typically telling misjudgement).

I see this mistake made a lot by critics of the film.

You won't get anything out of the film if you don't look at the film's depiction of middle class resentment.

The central dynamic is more Michael Gove/David Cameron than anyone else, especially if you have read Tim Shipman's Brexit book (and specifically his connections between Evelyn Waugh and the anti-establishment movement).

She is making the point - a valid one in the wake of Brexit - that so many of these so-called cultural revolutions are driven by white middle-class resentment, which leave outsiders and the lower classes vulnerable.

Ditto with Michael Gove, who worked hard to make his place at the centre of Government but was eventually seen to be a snake by the upper classes (Cameron and his wife, specifically) as well as the middle and lower classes whom he betrayed.

We also see this in the portrayals of the servants of Saltburn, who truly despise him.

An oxymoron.
